speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I particularly enjoyed the comments on this bill from the member opposite.
As a follow-up to a question I put to the member for Regina-Qu'Appelle, I would be interested in this member's comments on the point I made about the need to
Government Orders
have a conversion developed in this country. This would be a means by which, in a very realistic way, we would have a chance to get out of the arms race, giving those people working in these industries an opportunity to work in other areas that could be developed.
I think that is important. The author of a very important book entitled The Rise and Fall of Great Nations of the World made the point that one of the reasons Japan, as an example, was able to develop such a dynamic economy and put considerable resources into developing trade in its technological and automobile industries was that it did not have to allocate all those funds to armed forces.
Clearly, if it is not guns, it is butter. If a country allocates or spends in Canada some $1.5 billion annually on arms, I would be interested in knowing the member's views on conversion. What ideas does the government have on how to redirect some of those funds so that we could get out of the arms race and have people employed in the peace sector.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have to recognize that Canada is not a very big player in the manufacturing of arms. We are a minor player in that field in that we do not produce on a mass level a high volume of offensive arms. We are mainly engaged in producing conventional weapons that are used for defence.
In this case the two industries that we are talking about, Diemaco and GM, are supplying the Canadian army with light vehicles and the type of weapons that are used normally in defensive action.
Those two industries, based in Ontario and employing several hundred people, would not survive by supplying only the Canadian army.
We have an opportunity to sell some of those products to friendly countries and maintain those high quality jobs in high technology.
The government would be ill-advised not to take this opportunity to enhance those jobs and solidify those two companies and their contractors.
As for the conversion aspect of my colleague's question, I certainly appreciate and agree that we should be

May 30, 1991
Government Orders
looking at ways to augment and increase jobs in our production capacity in more society-oriented products. However, since there is a market and we still have a limited capacity to access that market, the country and the government should put every effort possible together to give our manufacturing firms access to those markets in order to consolidate their base and maintain the jobs that exist in those plants at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the hon. member's response to the question put by the member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley. I find it very interesting that he says he wants to enhance those jobs and solidify the positions of the two companies, but on the other hand he agrees that we might want to think at some time in the future about changing the role of those workers and changing the direction of those companies.
If we, as Canadians, do not agree with being in the arms race, and if we genuinely want to ensure that those workers have jobs, would it not make sense that at the same time as this government allows these contracts to be let that it begins to do some serious planning about conversion of those jobs into peace-type jobs as opposed to jobs that create war machines?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Mission-Coquitlam for her question and her comments. Of course, we should be very careful not to put the country in a position where we would have to import the arms that our forces may need in the future to provide the defence of our country and to help them to fulfil the role that from time to time we will ask them to perform for the United Nations.
We should maintain in Canada a basic industrial manufacturing capacity for the type of conventional arms that our forces will need. If we do not maintain that position, one day Canada will be a net importer, a net buyer of that type of weapon. That would put in jeopardy our balance of payments, create hardship in the economy and lose jobs. I personally think that we have to maintain a level of manufacturing capacity in Canada that will assure that we can equip our Armed Forces with the type of equipment they need to perform the job that we ask them to perform.
On the other hand, we should, as the government is doing, look at alternatives, look at ways to diversify the economy in order to create the type of jobs that will benefit the Canadian economy.
I repeat, we should be very careful not to put ourselves in a position where we will have to buy the equipment we need to ensure our security.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to rise in this very important debate which we are undertaking today. Some of the most eloquent and cogent arguments I have heard on this subject in many years of following the debate on arms control and the questions of disarmament have come in the debate today.
I would like to compliment very much a number of my colleagues whom I see seated around me, particularly the member for Trinity-Spadina, the member for Regina- Qu'Appelle and others who have spoken very eloquently. I would hope that this debate reaches far beyond the limited confines of this Chamber and becomes a debate throughout Canada. It is a very important debate, one of the most important debates perhaps that we have engaged in yet, although its subject matter may seem on the surface to be relatively mundane.
What startles me the most, and has startled many of us, is the utter hypocrisy of what we are witnessing today. Many of us who were involved in the gulf war debate in January, when we were called back to debate the resolution supporting United Nations action, will remember the government saying repeatedly that the situation in the Middle East was indeed the result of actions in the past. Weapons had been sold to people who clearly should not have had them.
There were repeated references made to the fact that Saddam Hussein had been allowed, in fact encouraged, to build up a massive armaments inventory in order to counteract the growing threat of the Ayatollah in Iran some years previously. The government repeatedly assured us that our fears about engaging in the gulf war were not grounded, that what we were doing was preparing for a new world order in which these kind of conflicts would no longer take place. The government said that after the gulf war the nations of the world would see to it that a new world order was established in which weapons of destruction would no longer be circu-
May 30, 1991

Government Orders
lated or sold, that mechanisms would be put in place to control the sale of arms and that we need no longer worry.
The government said to us if only we would support its position on the gulf war, if only we would support the position of the United Nations-speaking essentially for the United States-that this war was necessary, afterward everything would be all right. We would no longer need to fear the effects of the arms race.
In fact, in the period immediately following the war, the government, seeking to assure Canadians of that, went so far as to issue statements such as the following. On March 8, the then Secretary of State for External Affairs said:
The world cannot let a victory become a truce, an occasion for nations to rearm, regroup and return to battle. The peace which now beckons-must become a pattern.
He went on to say that to have peace in the Middle East region would require addressing the full spectrum of problems including, and I quote:
The proliferation of weapons of mass destruction, the arms trade, the constant chase for spheres of influence.
He then went on to describe how weapons used by Iraq were supplied largely by the five members of the Security Council: Britain, France, U.S., China and the U.S.S.R., the very people who sanctioned and, indeed, spearheaded the effort to fight that Gulf War. They in fact were fighting against their own weapons.
Following that we all remember that our own Prime Minister took the opportunity when President Bush was making his visit to our nation's capital to say to President Bush very clearly, and I quote:
There's a general view-without getting into the question of total interdiction for the moment - that clearly a lot of these weapons, to understate the case, fell into hands that should never have had them in the first place. We could be much more active in that area if we wanted. We have all the technology in the world; we have all the resources we need. We could be big arms merchants; we've chosen not to be, although it is a very lucrative business.
"We have chosen not to be because it is fundamentally inconsistent with our policy to develop it, to peddle it, to finance it, and then to deplore its use".
It is very hard to believe that the government led by the people who made those statements would now be proposing Bill C-6. It would vastly increase the scope and the range of weaponry which Canada peddles in the world.
It is very hard to believe that the government should be coming forward with this bill when we heard statements during that war that these kinds of wars are inevitable if weapons are allowed to build up and the arms trade is allowed to flourish because these weapons must sooner or later be used. I recall very clearly during the gulf war, because it startled me so much, an expert on weaponry and the arms trade discussing the issue on one of the many TV programs. The expert was asked whether in fact the war would have any impact on Canadian arms exports, and whether there was an opportunity there for arms manufacturers and exporters as a result of the war. The answer that this arms trade expert gave was that there would in fact be no sales as a result of the war because this was an inventory war.
I recall very clearly, as we all do, seeing signs in different stores in our communities where we come from indicating that there is an inventory sale. They have too many shoes. They have to clean out their inventory or whatever the commodity is. Here we got to the point where we had to have an inventory war because there were so many weapons awash in that region that sooner or later the temptation to use them became overwhelming.
We have had our inventory war. We have had our commitments from the government that we were in fact going to seek a new world order based on limiting very dramatically the flow of arms around the world. But what do we get? We get Bill C-6 and we see the Minister for International Trade, when he was defending the introduction of this bill, and other members from the government who have defended the bill before us, saying there are essentially two reasons why we have to adopt this particular piece of legislation. One is that they need to protect the jobs in the industry and the other argument is that in fact they are not weapons of mass destruction. Really all they are saying when they talk about arms control is that the methods of mass destruction and these particular weapons that would be affected by this bill will not be included in it.

May 30, 1991
Government Orders
Let me deal with those arguments for just a minute. First there is the question of jobs. Certainly I do not want to underestimate the importance of jobs in our economy. I do not want to see people unemployed who currently work in the armaments industry any more than I want to see farmers thrown off their farms. I do not want to see aboriginal people whose traditional lifestyles are being undermined forced to go on welfare.
I have particular feelings for this case because in 19741 was a candidate for my party in the constituency of London East where the GM plant that is to build these weapons is located. Many of the brothers and sisters in Local 27 of the UAW are good friends of mine and I know them well. Clearly they are concerned about the loss of jobs, and well they should be.
I would like to say to those brothers and sisters in Local 27 that they are not in fact the victims of a move by the opposition to curb the arms race or to unrealistically restrict a legitimate trade in these kinds of things but rather they are victims of a whole trend which we see more and more of.
A lot of that trend is wrapped around the whole question of free trade. Certainly the concern that people feel in southwestern Ontario about the loss of jobs stems directly from the fact that there are not alternate jobs or economic opportunities in that region because of the massive devastation wreaked on that region by the free trade agreement with the United States.
Second, I think it is symbolic of the fact that we are more and more integrating our economies between Canada and the United States, and a big part of that integration will inevitably mean in my opinion that we will become more and more involved in the arms trade. That is a result of the fact that the United States depends very heavily on the arms trade. Its economy is based in large measure, in far too great a measure many Americans and many other people in the world believe, on the arms trade. We are very rapidly coming to the same position.
Many of us have seen the arguments. Even when it comes to things like Minute Man missiles and other weapons of mass destruction, we see feature stories on television and read articles in the papers about citizens of communities in California, in Georgia, and other places that depend very heavily on the arms industry. We see stories that these people will lose their jobs, that
whole communities are in danger of being wiped out. Therefore it becomes a rationale to continue even the most appalling kinds of weapons manufacture. Those kinds of things are rationalized by the need for jobs, and we are getting closer and closer to that.
The other aspect of the whole free trade philosophy involved here is the commitment and the orientation toward viewing things only in terms of the bottom line. If there is a market opportunity, if there is a buck to be made, we have to be there. That is the free trade philosophy and that is the philosophy that we are seeing today.
The second argument the minister made was that these are not weapons of mass destruction, that these LAVs, these light armoured vehicles, are really a veiy insignificant kind of weapon. Let me read a little bit about the particular weapon that we are talking about:
The light armoured vehicle is a multi-role small tank on wheels, built to operate in a wide range of environments. It is amphibious, relatively fast, capable of moving up to 63 miles an hour on a road, can climb steep slopes, can be air-lifted or dropped by transport aircraft and helicopters. In its many variations, all of which are included in the Saudi sale, it can be used as a troop carrier, a communications command centre, a towing vehicle, a mortar launcher or an anti-tank weapon.
When I see things like "having the capability of being a mortar launcher or a communications command centre", we are not talking about something that is removed from warfare that includes mass destruction. We are talking in fact about a weapon that can be very integral to warfare, including weapons of mass destruction, as we saw very clearly in the gulf war where 250 of these vehicles were used by the United States military in their operations.
There is another aspect that disturbs me about these weapons being pooh-poohed as not being weapons of mass destruction and therefore not significant. This is the fact of what will necessarily happen when we sell these to various governments with dubious human rights records and with very poor records of allowing their citizenry to have influence in the affairs of then-countries. I think we are going to see that they will be used on a widespread scale for putting down civil disturbances.
In other words, we will see people like Saddam Hussein, or the leadership in Syria, or other countries such as that, using this weaponry to quell civil disturbances, to further oppress their own people and to
May 30, 1991

further perpetuate the kind of power that they already have.
I cannot see that allowing countries with these kinds of regimes to obtain this kind of weaponry for the purpose of quelling their own populations represents a step forward for Canada in any way.
The third problem I see here is that it will become even more tempting to get involved in all kinds of Third World trouble, to pursue a strategy of intervention in Third World disputes, and in fact to foment those Third World disputes if the whole question of spheres of influence and control by the superpowers is in some way threatened.
I see this very much as being part of a new world order that might not be so much based on mutual assured destruction, the old theory of having a balance of nuclear forces. That theory is being eclipsed by the end of the cold war. What we are seeing is a new world order based very much on strategic interventions all over the world with just as destructive an effect, and perhaps more destructive because there is much less public outcry when these kinds of interventions are made.
Further, I would like to speak about the arms race in general. We had all hoped when the cold war began to thaw, when it became clear that the old power blocs were disintegrating, that there might well be a peace dividend that would accrue to the world and that would be a benefit to the world's people.
We are cutting budgets here by 5, 10, 15 per cent and saying that the activities of departments thus cut will not be affected. We are talking about a cut of 2 to 4 per cent in the arms trade which would yield over $200 trillion in the next decade. When we are talking about countries with per capita incomes of $150, $300 or $500 a year, $200 trillion is a massive amount of money. It seems quite ironic that we should be talking about increasing the arms trade while at the same time we are cutting foreign aid from our own country.
Furthermore, I would like to make the argument that the arms trade has been a big factor in creating many of the current economic problems we see world-wide. Certainly the high interest regime we have just come through has been directly related to the arms trade. There are very many credible economists who have said that the inflationary interest rate spiral we were in was
Government Orders
fuelled directly by Ronald Reagan's arms build-up during his 1980 to 1988 regime and that our own economy has suffered as a result. We are hearing arguments continuously that we have to absorb the kind of Draconian economic measures here because of high interest rates. In fact, those high interest rates were fuelled originally by the arms race.
The arms race has created a situation where very, very poor countries are in a position where they are almost forced to devote huge percentages of their Gross National Product and of their national budgets to support buying armaments to defend against others who have had arms sold to them, their neighbours and so on. Therefore, there are situations in Central America, the Middle East, and elsewhere, where poor countries are devoting huge amounts of money to the arms trade. First of all, the only thing they can afford to do in their own countries is starve their own people. Second, when they import from other countries they are importing armaments instead of other very useful commodities which we could be exporting to them.
I am worried as well about Canada's international credibility. We have consistently taken a good line when it comes to arms control, when it comes to search for peace around the world, and for new mechanisms to ensure that a new world order would be a peaceful world order. But what does it do to Canada's credibility when, so quickly after a major war which should have taught us a lesson, we are out there flogging weapons with the best of them? Surely the countries around the world that look to Canada for leadership must be very, very disappointed when they see Canada leaping with both feet into what it sees to be a small commercial opportunity, the way we are doing here.
I see you are telling me that my time has almost expired. In closing, I would like to quote a few words from a former Conservative member of Parliament from Edmonton, Douglas Roche, who was Canada's ambassador for disarmament from 1984 to 1988. Certainly members from all sides of the House recognize Doug Roche as one of the most articulate and committed people when it comes to the whole question of disarmament.
He said:
The government is rushing this legislation, trying to get it passed before the summer recess. Public opinion ought quickly to be mounted to fortify opposition efforts to defeat the bill. It was public opinion that stopped Canada from joining the U.S. Star Wars initiative, that

May 30, 1991
Government Orders
stopped West German arms manufacturers from settling in Cape
Breton, that stopped the acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines.
Bill C-6 is another watershed moment. It must be killed.
I agree with those sentiments. I would hope that the public of Canada becomes aware very quickly of what is happening here, that the public of Canada will make its views known very quickly to the Government of Canada and to all members of Parliament. We cannot afford to proceed with this legislation. We will be forever branded as hypocrites if we do.

Mr. Speaker, last Thursday in this House I informed the minister responsible for Canada Post about the fight being waged by the community of Avonmore, Ontario, to keep its post office. Avonmore has had a post office since Confederation. It is sadly ironic that it will soon be closed at a time when Canada is seeking to preserve national unity and its federal symbols.
On May 23 over 60 residents of Avonmore stood on the steps in front of the House of Commons and held a rally to save their post office. They presented a petition with over 700 signatures, calling upon the government to rescind its decision to close their post office on June 27.
They also gave me a children's petition. It showed that the whole community has come together to voice its objections over the callous action taken by Canada Post to close the Avonmore post office.
The community of Avonmore feels betrayed by Canada Post. It is frustrated and angry that it was simply told that it was going to lose its post office and there was nothing it could do to stop it. As far as the people of Avonmore are concerned, their meeting with Canada Post representatives was a sham, nothing more than a farce.
The point I want to make today concerns the issue I was trying to get across to the minister responsible for Canada Post in my question to him last Thursday. That is, Avonmore will not only lose its post office, it will also not receive a retail postal outlet. There is only one store in the community and the owner does not want to have an RPO.
Canada Post has informed the people of Avonmore that it will be installing mailboxes when the post office is closed. However, this means that to register a letter or buy a stamp, the people of Avonmore will have to travel over 24 kilometres to the nearest post office. Postal service in Avonmore will therefore be considerably downgraded when the post office is closed.
The people of Avonmore should not have to leave their community and travel 24 kilometres to obtain such basic services as the ability to buy a stamp. This is totally unacceptable. It is a blatant contravention of Canada Post's promise to rural Canadians.
In June, 1988, Canada Post placed full-page ads in newspapers across Canada emphasizing, in its own words, that it would be "keeping our commitment to rural Canada". The ad stated that, and I am quoting: "Canada's rural communities are vital to Canada Post. In fact, one of the most important parts of our commitment is making postal products and services more accessible to rural Canadians".
This ad was nothing short of deception and propaganda. It went on to state that the corporation's commitment to its customers "will be to maintain and improve service as we evolve". Well, something must have gone terribly wrong during the evolution process. Canada Post's pledge to provide equal or better service when a post office is closed is not worth much to the people of Avonmore.
For all Canada Post and this government cares, the residents of Avonmore and other rural Canadians, who have no post office or shining RPO to serve them, could travel over 100 kilometres to buy a stamp. As long as the
May 30, 1991

master plan to eliminate over 5,200 rural post offices by 1996 goes ahead, the government and the corporation will be happy.
In conclusion, the people of rural Canada feel betrayed. Luckily they will have an opportunity to throw a monkey wrench into the master plan long before 1996. The government has ignored rural Canadians far too long. As a result, it will be the government that will be closed down come the next election, closed down in the very same quick and harsh manner in which the people of Avonmore will lose their post office.

Mr. Speaker, about two weeks ago I raised with the minister of defence speculation in the press that the government was considering closing Armed Forces bases across the country and two bases that we now operate and have operated for some time in Europe.
This speculation has gone on for some time. It has gone on in the complete absence of any defence policy in this country whatsoever. In 1987, when the last white paper was written, it was out of date. It is even more out of date at this time. We have been operating all this time with absolutely no defence policy in Canada or no indication of the date when a defence policy may be brought forward.
Yet we go on with ad hockery in this country. We go on with the administration of defence by the Department of Finance. There are $2.5 billion worth of cuts in the last budget. This was the most severe cut to any department probably in Canadian history and certainly the most severe cut that the Canadian forces have received for some time. However, rule by the department of defence is no way to create a defence policy for this country. It is incumbent on the Government of Canada to bring forward a policy so that the people of Canada, who are now discussing the Constitution, who are now discussing native rights, will also be able to discuss how they want sovereignty to be maintained in this country and how they want security exercised in this country.
It is 1991 now and it is time not only for the government to bring forward suggestions as to the direction they want to go, but to engage the Canadian people in a public debate on those very directions.
What makes the lack of policy at this time even more reprehensible is the fact that Canadian forces have just performed well in the gulf. They performed with professionalism, they performed with competence, and they deserve better. They deserve better, as do the people

May 30, 1991
Adjournment Debate
who work at the bases we have all across this country. There are hundreds of thousands of people in Canada now whose jobs depend on those bases, either directly or indirectly, and it is not fair in a time of economic recession to keep them in suspense, to keep them in concern and in distress, and in worry about their future and the future of their jobs. That is not the way to run the country. We had the example of Summerside, where a whole province was affected very negatively by the closing of one base. There are areas of this country that depend very, very much on the presence of the Armed Forces to create jobs, particularly in areas of the country normally referred to as have not areas, less developed areas of the country.
It is important, when that policy is brought forward and when the closure of bases is contemplated, that economic and social aspects be taken into consideration. We did not see that before. Before, when the government closed bases in Canada, it used an axe where a scalpel would have been desirable. We probably do not need all bases across this country. My colleague from Toronto even called for the closing of Downsview in Toronto, and yet Downsview continues to survive and prosper in spite of the need for land, for development, and for housing in that community. It mystifies those of us on this side.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is aware that the minister and his department have undertaken an extensive consultation process with the people who are involved in the cross-border shopping issue.
We have to deal with it, and we are dealing with it through consultation with the stakeholders, including all three levels of government, the private sector, labour and consumer organizations, and we are making headway toward a better understanding of the complexity of the situation and needs for specific solutions.
The Minister of National Revenue has spent a great deal of time and effort ensuring that we find more efficient and effective ways of dealing with this matter. There is no one solution to this complex problem, and I think the hon. member knows this. What may well be appropriate for eastern Ontario border locations may well be inappropriate for others. As the hon. member is no doubt aware, the minister and departmental officials at all levels have been meeting with local mayors, provincial government officials, and other concerned parties to ensure that the solutions for each border office are tailored to the needs of the community served.
Canada Customs continues to perform a delicate balancing act between enforcement and protection of Canada's borders while, at the same time, providing efficient service to the travelling public.
I would emphasize that only through consultation with members of local interest groups can we come up with well thought out solutions to the varied concerns of border communities. I would urge the member to encourage his constituents to join with business, labour, governments, and consumers in dealing with this issue.

Mr. Speaker, I rose yesterday, May 29, to ask a question of the Minister of Transport and that question was: Would he include a purchase clause in the lease agreement? In other words, would he make the lease agreement for the transfer of the Edmonton International Airport to the local authority a lease to purchase agreement?
He gave me the answer: "No." He did not want to privatize the airport. He missed the question because I was not talking about privatization. I was merely asking that a purchase clause be inserted into the lease agreement so that at some point in the future the local authority, the Edmonton Airport Authority, could exercise an option or negotiate with the federal government to take over the international airport.
The reason this is important is that when the local authority will lease the airport, it will put $10 million a year into infrastructure improvements each year for 10 years. It wants a little certainty about whether the return will come to it after this time. Also the people who will lend the money to the Edmonton airport authority would like some certainty as to who is to own the assets after this 10-year period. Having a lease agreement only is not very workable now.
May 30, 1991

In fact, I would like to quote a consultant which the federal government consulted on this issue. The consultant, the Royal Bank of Canada, said: "We believe it is much cleaner to avoid these issues entirely by leaving ownership of the assets with the federal government indefinitely". They would like to have the assets owned by the federal government indefinitely. They would like a reversion clause in the lease agreement so all the infrastructure improvements might revert back to the federal government.
This is very unfair to the local authority. The government wanted to privatize it at first. It was realized that maybe some local authorities might fail and the government might wish to take it back. The government started out with a lease to purchase option. In fact, the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada went to Edmonton in 1989 and signed a memorandum of agreement for a lease to purchase. T\vo years later the purchase option was taken out.
I would like an answer tonight whether the parliamentary secretary, the member for Calgary Southeast, will make a commitment to ask the Minister of Transport to put a purchase option into the lease agreement. It will not cost them anything. It is just an option that the two of them get together near the end of the lease to discuss terms and allow the airport authority to take over and purchase the airport after it has put in $100 million or more worth of infrastructure improvements.
The building is now 30 years old and a consultant hired by the local airport authority has said the building might have to be replaced. Transport Canada has been very negligent in the upkeep of the building and it is very important.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the member if he will make a commitment to go to the Minister of Transport and have this clause added.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the hon. member's question and also his efforts on behalf of his constituents in Edmonton to get involved in the negotiations between the department and the local airport authority.
However, my hon. friend may not be aware of all the background that went into the developing of the government's position regarding lease versus sale. I can assure
Adjournment Debate
the hon. member that the matter was thoroughly examined and not just by bureaucrats.
As you may recall, when the government approved the principles for the creation and operation of local airport authorities in May, 1989, it gave a specific negotiating mandate to the Minister of Transport. This mandate states that the airports are to be transferred on terms to be negotiated to newly created community based nonprofitable organizations, the local airport authorities. In other words, they were not to be privatized.
This is not to say that the transfer will disregard sound business principles. On the contrary, the mandate also requires that the airports be transferred on the basis of fair market value with appropriate consideration for their future earning potential.
Finally, the government, not the department, decided for several reasons that negotiations were to be initiated on the basis of transfer by way of long-term lease for a number of reasons.
For one, it was felt that the sale of airports to new and unproven business organizations might be seen by the public as putting at risk these essential elements of our transportation infrastructure.
As the hon. member noted, early in 1989 Transport Canada's airport transfer task force retained the corporate finance division of the Royal Bank of Canada to report on the financing for local airport authorities. The report considered the question of lease versus sale from the perspective of lenders and investors and took into account the legal, financial, and perceptual implications.
To put it succinctly, the Royal Bank found that from a technical perspective for financiers, it does not matter if the airport authority owns or leases the property and assets as long as it has the unfettered right to use the facilities and, more importantly, the authority to generate revenues from the airport's assets.
They also concluded that they believed it to be preferable in Canada for the airports to be leased to the local airport authorities rather than sold.
I can also add that the conclusion that leasing is preferable to an outright sale has been strongly endorsed by the airport authority advisory board. This board was constituted in 1989 to provide the Minister of Transport with advice from a private sector perspective on all aspects of the airport transfer initiative.

May 30, 1991
Adjournment Debate
Officials at Transport Canada and the Department of Justice are meeting regularly with the four local airport authorities and I believe that progress has been made within the framework set out by the government.
The hon. member's interest in this matter is most appreciated, and I sincerely hope that my comments have alleviated his concern.
